lesson_title: A Sheet of Paper That Holds a Textbook
hook_text: Flat, it cannot hold one coin. Rolled, it holds a textbook. Folded, it holds a cup of coins. Same paper.
clip_script: Lay a sheet of A4 across a gap between two books. It droops. Add one coin and it falls through. Now roll an identical sheet into a tube, tape it, and lay it across the same gap. Pile coins into a cup on top. Dozens. Stand it on end and it holds a textbook. Fold a third sheet into a sharp zigzag along its length: it carries a cupful too. Same paper, same weight, no glue, no extra material. The paper did not get stronger. It got stiffer, because a flat sheet bends easily when all its material sits in one thin layer, and a tube or a fold moves that material away from the middle, where it has to stretch and squash to let the bend happen. Turn the folds the wrong way and it collapses: folds must run along the span. Look around: drinking straws, bicycle frames, bones, corrugated roofs, cardboard, car floors. Free stiffness, everywhere. Your tower legs should be tubes.
visual_style: Whiteboard three sheets side by side, flat sagging, rolled with coins stacked on it, pleated with coins; arrows showing stretch and squash on the tube wall.
mood: Delighted surprise, a cheap trick that explains half the built world.
pacing: Three quick tests, the one-sentence explanation, the wrong-way fold, a rapid list of examples.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run the three paper tests at home with a cup of coins.
